weaknesses: Reliance on Structured Metadata: FAMAE fundamentally relies on the availability of structured, engineered feature fields (e.g., categorical hierarchies). It is unclear how the framework would adapt to domains where items are primarily defined by unstructured raw text or images, which is where LLM-based approaches typically shine.

Downstream Training Efficiency: As acknowledged in the limitations, while the tokenization stage is highly efficient, the downstream generative model (G-stage) still relies on a standard autoregressive Transformer (T5), which suffers from slow convergence compared to traditional item-ID based models.
questions_for_authors: How does ReSID perform in scenarios with highly sparse or completely unstructured metadata (e.g., only raw text descriptions)? Can FAMAE be naturally extended to incorporate unstructured modalities without reverting to the semantic-centric LLM pipeline?

In GAOQ, could the enforcement of globally shared orthogonal anchors force unnatural code assignments if the intrinsic geometric distribution of child clusters differs drastically across different parent nodes?

summary_of_contributions: The paper introduces FlattenGPT, a novel two-stage depth compression framework for Large Language Models (LLMs). In the first stage, it addresses the redundancy in deep transformer blocks by 'flattening' highly similar adjacent layers, effectively merging them by concatenating their multi-head attention and MLP parameters. In the second stage, it applies channel pruning (removing attention heads and using Nyström approximation for MLP channels) to reduce the widened block back to its original dimensions. The authors claim this approach bridges the gap between depth and width compression, preserving the knowledge of all layers while maintaining a uniform, hardware-friendly architecture and achieving superior performance-efficiency trade-offs compared to existing methods.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are well-supported by both theoretical analysis and extensive empirical evidence. The authors theoretically motivate the cross-layer similarity using the 'curse of depth' (feature variance and gradient norms). Empirically, the method is evaluated on LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, and Baichuan-2, consistently outperforming recent depth compression baselines (e.g., SLEB, ShortGPT, LaCo) in both zero-shot accuracy and WikiText-2 perplexity. The throughput and latency measurements validate the claim that the resulting uniform architecture retains the acceleration benefits of depth compression. One limitation in the evidence is the heavy reliance on a single sparsity ratio (~20-24%); the paper lacks a comprehensive Pareto curve showing how the method scales at higher compression rates.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper is excellently situated within the literature. It clearly distinguishes its approach from entire-block pruning (which suffers from severe information loss) and standard channel pruning (which fails to reduce depth and creates irregular architectures). The idea of converting depth redundancy into width redundancy before pruning is a conceptually elegant synthesis of prior layer-merging and width-compression techniques.
strengths: Conceptual Elegance: The core idea of 'flattening' depth into width to prevent the catastrophic information loss associated with dropping entire layers is highly principled and offers a deep insight into transformer representation capacity.

Strong Empirical Results: The method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art training-free depth compression baselines across a diverse set of modern LLMs (LLaMA, Qwen, Baichuan) and scales successfully to 70B parameter models.

Practicality: By ensuring the final pruned blocks match the original architectural dimensions, FlattenGPT produces models that are immediately compatible with existing hardware optimizations and deployment infrastructures.
weaknesses: Limited Sparsity Exploration: The evaluations are almost exclusively conducted at a ~20% sparsity level. A continuous ablation or Pareto curve evaluating performance at higher compression ratios (e.g., 30%, 40%, 50%) is necessary to understand the breaking point of the flattening operation.

Incremental Second Stage: While the layer flattening is highly novel, the specific channel pruning techniques employed in the second stage (Nyström approximation) are standard. A deeper analysis of how these specific techniques interact with the flattened representations would strengthen the paper.
questions_for_authors: Can you provide a Pareto curve or additional results showing the trade-off between perplexity/accuracy and higher sparsity ratios (e.g., 30%, 40%, 50%)? At what point does the flattening approach experience catastrophic degradation?

When pruning the flattened layers, did you observe any patterns regarding which parameters are preserved? For instance, does the pruning algorithm tend to favor attention heads or MLP channels from the earlier layer or the later layer of the merged pair?
Does the temporary doubling of parameters during the flattening stage introduce any significant memory bottlenecks during the pruning process, particularly for the 70B model?

summary_of_contributions: The paper introduces FlattenGPT, a novel two-stage, training-free depth compression method for Large Language Models. To address the severe performance degradation caused by entirely dropping 'redundant' transformer blocks (standard depth compression), the authors propose 'flattening' two highly similar adjacent blocks into a single parallel block that is twice as wide. In the second stage, the method applies channel pruning (head removal for MHA, Nyström approximation for MLP) to reduce the widened block back to the original architectural dimensions. This approach reduces model depth (yielding proportional latency improvements) while preserving a synthesized mix of knowledge from both original blocks. Experiments demonstrate superior perplexity and zero-shot task performance compared to existing depth and width compression techniques across several LLM families (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2).
claims_and_evidence: The core claims regarding performance retention and latency improvements are well-supported by robust empirical evidence across diverse models and established baselines. The experimental design is sound, utilizing standard zero-shot benchmarks, perplexity metrics, and actual throughput/latency measurements. However, the claim that flattening 'preserves all knowledge' is slightly overstated, as the subsequent 50% channel pruning inherently discards information, though empirically it is demonstrably better than discarding 100% of a single layer. Additionally, the theoretical analysis (Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2) largely reiterates the 'curse of depth' findings from very recent prior work (Sun et al., 2025) rather than introducing a fundamentally new theoretical framework.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper contextualizes itself excellently within the current model compression landscape. It accurately distinguishes its approach from both traditional depth compression (layer dropping, e.g., ShortGPT, SLEB) and width compression (channel pruning, e.g., SliceGPT, LLM-Pruner). It also appropriately contrasts its approach with simple layer merging (e.g., LaCo). The literature review is comprehensive, though the reliance on Sun et al. (2025) for the theoretical motivation could be more explicitly framed as an application of their theory rather than a novel derivation.
strengths: Visionary Approach to Compression: The core idea of transforming depth compression into a width compression problem via layer flattening is highly innovative. It beautifully bridges the latency benefits of depth pruning with the performance retention of channel pruning.

Hardware and Deployment Friendly: By pruning the widened layers exactly back to their original dimensions, FlattenGPT maintains a uniform, standard transformer architecture. This is a massive advantage for real-world deployment, as it allows the compressed model to seamlessly utilize existing highly-optimized inference kernels (e.g., FlashAttention, vLLM) without custom engineering.

Strong Empirical Performance and Efficiency: The method achieves state-of-the-art results for training-free pruning, significantly outperforming existing layer-dropping techniques. Furthermore, the pruning process itself is computationally lightweight (taking only minutes on a single GPU), making it highly practical.
weaknesses: Heuristic Layer Selection: The iterative greedy algorithm for layer selection (Algorithm 1) relies on manually modifying the similarity matrix (deleting rows/columns) to prevent merging too many consecutive layers. This heuristic feels somewhat ad-hoc and lacks a rigorous guarantee of finding the optimal global sequence of merges.

Overstated Theoretical Contribution: Sections 2.2 and Appendix A lean heavily on existing proofs from Sun et al. (2025). While providing good context for why deep layers are redundant, this section is presented as a novel theoretical contribution when it is mostly a recapitulation of the known 'curse of depth'.

Lack of Generative Evaluation: While zero-shot classification and perplexity are standard, evaluating the pruned models on modern generative reasoning tasks (e.g., MT-Bench, AlpacaEval, or GSM8K) is becoming the gold standard. It remains unclear how the 'mixed-knowledge' representation in the flattened layers affects the model's long-form coherence and reasoning capabilities.
questions_for_authors: Can you clarify the specific theoretical novelty of Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 compared to the cited work by Sun et al. (2025)?

In Algorithm 1, deleting rows/columns to prevent merging consecutive layers acts as a hard constraint. Did you experiment with softer penalties for consecutive merges, or dynamic programming approaches to find the optimal global sequence of merges?

How does FlattenGPT perform on generative benchmarks (e.g., MT-Bench or GSM8K) compared to standard layer dropping? Does the integration of weights from two different layers into one cause any rotational or semantic mismatch that manifests during free-form generation?

When flattening MHA, you concatenate heads to form a 2H head layer, then prune back to H. Does this implicitly assume that the query/key projections from layer l-1 and l operate in the exact same representational subspace?

summary_of_contributions: The paper proposes FlattenGPT, a novel depth compression method for Large Language Models (LLMs). It addresses the performance degradation commonly seen in standard layer-dropping techniques by introducing a two-stage process: (1) 'Layer Flattening', which merges two highly similar adjacent transformer blocks by concatenating their attention heads and MLP channels, and (2) 'Channel Pruning', which compresses the widened block back to its original dimensions using an activation-based importance metric for MHA and Nyström approximation for the MLP. This approach allows the model to retain critical knowledge from both layers while achieving the inference speedups of depth compression and maintaining architectural consistency. Extensive experiments on LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, and Baichuan-2 demonstrate favorable perplexity and zero-shot performance trade-offs compared to prior depth and width pruning methods.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are generally well-supported by extensive empirical evidence. The authors evaluate across a diverse set of modern LLMs (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen, Baichuan) and show consistent improvements over strong baselines (ShortGPT, SLEB, LaCo, SliceGPT). The throughput and latency measurements validate the practical speedup claims. However, the theoretical claims in Section 2.2 (Lemma 2.1 and 2.2) regarding the 'curse of depth' rely heavily on recent prior work (Sun et al., 2025) and establish that deeper layers are redundant, which is already a widely accepted premise in depth pruning. The paper lacks a theoretical or deep empirical analysis specifically explaining *why* the channel pruning phase of FlattenGPT retains better knowledge than simply dropping the layer, though the end-to-end metrics support the final claim.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper is well-situated within the literature, adequately citing both depth compression (ShortGPT, SLEB, LaCo, BlockPruner) and width compression (LLM-Pruner, SliceGPT, SparseGPT, Wanda). The distinction between FlattenGPT (concatenation + pruning) and layer merging methods like LaCo (which adds/averages weights) is clear and empirically validated. The authors clearly bridge the gap between structured width pruning and layer dropping.
strengths: Conceptual Novelty: Bridging depth and width compression by conceptually 'flattening' adjacent layers into a wider layer and then applying channel pruning is a creative and highly effective approach. It avoids the catastrophic knowledge loss of pure layer-dropping.

Architectural Consistency: By pruning the flattened layer exactly back to its original dimensions, the method produces a drop-in replacement model that requires no custom CUDA kernels or hardware adjustments, maximizing practical utility.

Strong Empirical Results: The method is thoroughly evaluated on a wide range of state-of-the-art open-weight LLMs (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2) and consistently outperforms existing training-free depth and width pruning baselines in both perplexity and zero-shot tasks.

Practical Efficiency: The method is computationally efficient (taking only minutes to run the pruning stage on a single GPU) and translates to actual wall-clock speedups during inference (e.g., 1.27x throughput improvement at 20% sparsity).
weaknesses: Limited Insight into the Pruning Dynamics: While the method works well, the paper does not analyze the distribution of the retained heads/channels. When two layers are flattened and pruned by 50%, does the pruning algorithm tend to keep an equal mix of channels from layer l-1 and layer l, or does it effectively drop most of one layer? Understanding this would shed light on *why* flattening works better than layer dropping.

Heuristic Layer Selection: The iterative layer selection algorithm (Algorithm 1) modifies the similarity matrix by simply deleting rows/columns to prevent merging too many consecutive layers. This feels somewhat heuristic and could be better formalized or ablated.

Theoretical Disconnect: Section 2.2 provides proofs on gradient norms and variance (Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2), but these largely re-derive or heavily lean on Sun et al. (2025) to prove that deep layers are redundant. This theoretical motivation is somewhat generic to all depth-pruning methods and does not specifically analyze why the proposed flattening operation is mathematically superior.
questions_for_authors: Could you provide an analysis of the provenance of the retained channels/heads after the pruning stage? Specifically, what percentage of the retained MHA heads and MLP channels originate from layer l-1 versus layer l?

In Algorithm 1, the modification of the similarity matrix prevents certain consecutive merges. Have you ablated this specific heuristic? What happens to the performance if you simply use a standard dynamic programming approach to find the optimal non-overlapping pairs to merge?

How does FlattenGPT scale to higher compression ratios (e.g., 30% or 40% depth compression)? Does the performance start to degrade similarly to layer dropping once the pruning ratio within the flattened layers becomes too high?

summary_of_contributions: The paper proposes FlattenGPT, a novel depth compression method for Large Language Models. Instead of entirely dropping transformer layers, FlattenGPT merges two adjacent layers by concatenating their attention heads and MLP intermediate channels, which perfectly preserves their combined output. It then applies channel pruning (Nyström approximation for MLP, head-importance scoring for MHA) to reduce the merged layer back to the original width. This approach achieves the hardware efficiency of depth compression while retaining significantly more knowledge, outperforming existing training-free depth compression baselines on various LLMs.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are strongly supported by the empirical evidence. The experimental design is rigorous, comparing against a wide range of state-of-the-art width and depth compression techniques across multiple model families (LLaMA, Qwen, Baichuan). The mathematical formulation of the layer flattening step is exact and elegant. The only problematic claim is the presentation of Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2, which seem to be derived directly from a cited concurrent work (Sun et al., 2025) without explicit attribution in the main text.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper is well-situated within the model compression literature, effectively bridging the gap between depth compression (layer dropping/merging) and width compression (channel pruning). It compares favorably against recent methods like LaCo and SLEB. However, the theoretical analysis needs clearer attribution to Sun et al. (2025) in the main text.
strengths: Conceptual Elegance: The idea of flattening two transformer layers by concatenating their attention heads and MLP intermediate dimensions is mathematically sound. It exactly preserves the combined output of the two layers (as a sum) before pruning, providing a much better starting point for compression than dropping a layer entirely or averaging weights.

Strong Empirical Results: FlattenGPT significantly outperforms existing depth compression methods (e.g., SLEB, ShortGPT, LaCo) across multiple LLMs (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2) while maintaining the original architecture's hardware efficiency advantages.

Hardware Friendliness: By returning the merged layer to its original width, the method achieves actual wall-clock speedups without requiring specialized sparse kernels, making it highly practical for deployment.
weaknesses: Attribution of Theoretical Analysis: Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2 appear to be heavily based on or identical to results from Sun et al. (2025). While Sun et al. is cited in the preceding paragraph, the main text presents these lemmas as if they are the authors' original theoretical contributions. Proper attribution must be made explicit in the main text.

Ambiguity in Similarity Matrix Definition: In Section 3.1, the similarity matrix S_{i,j} is defined as the cosine similarity between the 'input feature of layer i and the output feature of layer j'. However, earlier text discusses the similarity of 'inputs of adjacent blocks'. If it is indeed input-to-output, the rationale should be clarified.

Greedy Layer Selection Heuristic: The heuristic for modifying the similarity matrix S after a merge (deleting row l and column l-1) is a bit hard to follow and lacks a strong mathematical justification, though it serves as a functional algorithmic constraint.
questions_for_authors: Could you clarify the exact relationship between Lemmas 2.1/2.2 and the findings in Sun et al. (2025)? Please ensure that the main text explicitly attributes these proofs if they are derived directly from prior work.

In Section 3.1, is S_{i,j} strictly the similarity between the *input* of layer i and the *output* of layer j? If so, doesn't S_{l-1, l} measure how well the combination of block l-1 and l approximates an identity mapping, rather than the similarity of their inputs? Please clarify the exact formulation and intuition.

The exact functional equivalence of the MLP concatenation (i.e., that the concatenated SwiGLU exactly equals the sum of the two original MLPs) is a very strong property of your method. Have you considered highlighting this exact mathematical equivalence more prominently in the text to emphasize why this is superior to weight-averaging methods like LaCo?

summary_of_contributions: The paper introduces FlattenGPT, a highly innovative depth compression framework for Large Language Models. Addressing the severe information loss inherent in traditional layer-dropping techniques, the authors propose a 'layer flattening' mechanism. Highly similar adjacent transformer blocks are merged into a single, widened block by concatenating their attention heads and MLP channels. This expanded block is subsequently compressed back to its original architectural dimensions using targeted channel pruning (head removal for MHA and Nyström approximation for the MLP). This approach effectively translates depth redundancy into width redundancy, preserving crucial learned representations while maintaining the original, hardware-friendly architectural dimensions. The method retains up to 96% of zero-shot performance at a 20% compression ratio across various LLMs.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are exceptionally well-supported by both theoretical formalization and rigorous empirical evidence. The authors provide a compelling theoretical grounding (Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2) demonstrating variance explosion and gradient vanishing, which plausibly explains the 'curse of depth' and the resulting cross-layer redundancy. The experimental design is highly insightful; specifically, the ablation study separating the 'flattening' step from the 'pruning' step beautifully illuminates the deeper mechanics of the network, proving that structural merging preserves knowledge (98% performance retention before pruning) while layer dropping destroys it.
relation_to_prior_work: The work brilliantly contextualizes itself at the intersection of depth compression (layer dropping) and width compression (channel pruning). It references key contemporary works (ShortGPT, SliceGPT, SLEB, LaCo) and successfully bridges these two domains. By demonstrating that depth reduction can be gracefully cast as a width reduction problem, the paper proposes a radically new mechanism that could inspire a paradigm shift in how the community approaches transformer compression.
strengths: Conceptual Breakthrough: The paper introduces a transformative 'squash and squeeze' paradigm. By merging layers via concatenation and then pruning, it transforms a destructive depth compression problem into a manageable width compression problem. This represents a radical and elegant shift from the binary 'keep or drop' layer pruning methods.

Theoretical Soundness: The reasoning is mathematically plausible and illuminating. The formalization of the 'curse of depth' (Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2) provides a rigorous justification for why deep transformer layers degenerate into identity mappings, grounding the empirical observation of cross-layer similarity in solid theory.

Experimental Insight: The experiments do more than just chase state-of-the-art numbers; they illuminate deeper aspects of learning. Figure 6, which compares layer pruning directly against layer flattening, is a profound experimental insight showing exactly where and why traditional depth compression fails.

Practical and Future Impact: Because the flattened and pruned blocks strictly match the original architectural dimensions, the method is inherently hardware-friendly and requires no custom CUDA kernels. This high practical utility, combined with its conceptual elegance, is likely to inspire widespread adoption and future research into structural transformations.
weaknesses: Dependence on Underlying Pruning Algorithms: While the flattening conceptualization is a breakthrough, the ultimate performance relies heavily on the efficacy of the secondary channel pruning step. The Nyström approximation is solid, but the paper leaves somewhat unexplored how more advanced, activation-aware, or gradient-based pruning mechanisms could push the performance ceiling even higher.

Generalization to Non-Standard Architectures: The theoretical and empirical framework is deeply tied to the standard Pre-LN Transformer architecture. It remains speculative how this flattening operation might adapt to emerging, complex architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) or Mamba-Transformer hybrids, though the authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation.
questions_for_authors: Could you elaborate on the computational scalability of the iterative layer selection process (Algorithm 1)? How does the cost of computing the similarity matrix scale for extremely deep models (e.g., 100+ layers)?

Have you experimented with flattening more than two adjacent layers into a single block before applying the pruning step? Would a 3-to-1 or 4-to-1 flattening yield a better compression-to-performance ratio for models with extreme depth redundancy?

How does the layer flattening operation alter the distribution of activation outliers? Specifically, would FlattenGPT be seamlessly compatible with Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) methods like AWQ or GPTQ, or does the merging of parameters exacerbate outlier magnitudes?

summary_of_contributions: The paper introduces FlattenGPT, a novel depth compression method for Large Language Models (LLMs). It addresses the performance degradation inherent in traditional layer-dropping techniques by proposing an elegant two-stage approach. First, it 'flattens' adjacent transformer blocks into a single, wider block by concatenating their parameters and hidden states. This exploits the high cross-layer similarity in deep networks to preserve learned knowledge. Second, it applies structured channel pruning (head pruning for MHA and Nystrom approximation for MLP) to compress the widened block back to its original architectural dimensions. This maintains strict architectural consistency while achieving the latency benefits of depth compression and the performance retention of width compression.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are well-supported by both theoretical analysis and empirical evidence. The authors theoretically analyze the growth of hidden state variance and gradient norms to justify cross-layer redundancy. Empirically, they demonstrate that FlattenGPT retains 90-96% of zero-shot performance on models like LLaMA-2/3 and Qwen-1.5 at a 20% sparsity ratio, outperforming existing depth compression baselines like SLEB and ShortGPT. Throughput and latency measurements on A100 GPUs provide convincing evidence of the method's practical hardware acceleration.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper effectively contextualizes its contribution within the realms of depth compression (layer dropping/merging) and width compression (channel pruning). It clearly articulates the limitations of prior depth compression methods (severe knowledge loss) and width compression methods (inconsistent architectures, lack of depth reduction). The comparison with state-of-the-art baselines such as SLEB, LaCo, ShortGPT, and SliceGPT is comprehensive and well-cited.
strengths: Elegance and Practicality: The proposed 'flatten-then-prune' pipeline is a highly elegant solution to the knowledge loss problem in depth compression. By restoring the original tensor dimensions, the method guarantees seamless deployment on existing AI accelerators without requiring custom kernels or complex hyperparameter tuning.

Theoretical Rigor: The authors provide a solid theoretical foundation explaining the curse of depth and why deep layers degenerate into identity mappings, perfectly motivating the flattening operation.

Robust Scalability: The empirical validation is comprehensive, demonstrating consistent performance retention and tangible latency improvements across a diverse and modern set of large-scale models (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, up to 70B parameters).
weaknesses: Compression Overhead: While inference is accelerated, the covariance matrix computation and Nystrom approximation during the offline compression phase may require significant memory for models with very large hidden dimensions, potentially limiting accessibility for practitioners with constrained hardware.

Sparsity Limits: The evaluation is mostly focused on ~20-25% sparsity. It remains unclear if this method scales gracefully to higher compression regimes (e.g., 40-50%) where multiple layers might need to be flattened into one.
questions_for_authors: Can you elaborate on the peak memory requirements during the offline compression phase, particularly for the 70B model? Does the Nystrom approximation become a memory bottleneck?
How does the method behave when pushed to higher sparsity levels (e.g., 40-50%)? Does the greedy layer selection algorithm still hold up when flattening multiple sequential layers?

summary_of_contributions: The paper proposes FlattenGPT, a novel two-stage depth compression methodology for Large Language Models (LLMs). Rather than entirely dropping redundant layers, FlattenGPT first 'flattens' highly similar adjacent transformer blocks into a single, wider block, effectively concatenating their parameters and preserving learned representations. In the second stage, it applies structured channel pruning (utilizing a Nyström approximation for MLPs and an activation-based importance metric for MHAs) to reduce the flattened layer back to the original architectural width. This approach successfully bridges depth and width compression, achieving higher hardware efficiency than pure channel pruning while retaining significantly better zero-shot performance and perplexity than baseline layer-dropping methods.
claims_and_evidence: The core claim that FlattenGPT provides a superior trade-off between inference speed (latency/throughput) and performance compared to existing depth and width compression techniques is well-supported by extensive experiments on LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, and Baichuan-2. The empirical evidence is robust. However, the theoretical claims regarding the 'curse of depth' (Lemmas 2.1 and 2.2) rely on the strong probabilistic assumptions that weights and intermediate hidden states follow independent normal distributions with a mean of zero. While mathematically sound under these assumptions, trained generative LLMs exhibit heavy-tailed weight distributions and massive activation outliers. Thus, the theoretical proofs serve more as a motivating toy model than a rigorous probabilistic framework for trained networks.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper elegantly positions itself at the intersection of depth compression (e.g., SLEB, ShortGPT) and width compression (e.g., SliceGPT, LLM-Pruner). It clearly articulates the limitations of both fields—depth compression losing too much information and width compression failing to reduce actual layer count/latency. The references are comprehensive. A minor missing context is the discussion of how such deterministic pruning methods impact the probabilistic calibration and generation diversity of the resulting models, which is an increasingly important area in generative AI literature.
strengths: The conceptual innovation of 'flattening' adjacent layers to preserve information before pruning is highly intuitive and elegantly bridges the gap between depth and width compression.

The use of the Nyström approximation for MLP channel pruning is mathematically rigorous, effectively minimizing the L2 reconstruction error of the activations and grounding the pruning step in solid statistical reasoning.
Strong empirical results across multiple modern LLM architectures, demonstrating superior perplexity and zero-shot performance compared to existing training-free pruning baselines.

From an application standpoint, maintaining strict architectural consistency (the same width and number of heads as the original model) makes this method highly practical for deployment on existing hardware and AI infrastructure. This directly advances the tractability of generative models, enabling deployment in resource-constrained, socially relevant domains (e.g., edge-device healthcare assistants) and promoting sustainable AI.
weaknesses: The probabilistic grounding in Section 2.2 assumes independent, normally distributed weights and hidden states. Trained LLMs are known to exhibit massive activation outliers and non-Gaussian properties, making this analysis somewhat disconnected from the empirical reality of the models being compressed.

The method relies on a very small calibration set (128 samples). While the ablation study suggests this is sufficient for deterministic performance metrics (accuracy/perplexity), it is unclear how this aggressive, low-data pruning affects the model's probabilistic outputs, such as predictive uncertainty, calibration, and generation diversity.

In Algorithm 1, the similarity matrix is modified heuristically (deleting rows/columns) to force adjacent-like merging. The probabilistic or theoretical justification for this specific routing heuristic is under-explored.
questions_for_authors: Could you discuss how the Gaussian and independence assumptions in Section 2.2 limit the theoretical analysis, especially given the well-documented presence of activation outliers in models like LLaMA?
How does FlattenGPT affect the predictive uncertainty and probabilistic calibration of the LLM? Do the pruned models become overconfident compared to the dense baselines?

Can you elaborate on the theoretical justification for the matrix modification heuristic in Algorithm 1? How does it guarantee optimal information flow compared to a more globally aware probabilistic routing mechanism?

summary_of_contributions: The paper proposes FlattenGPT, a novel two-stage depth compression method for Large Language Models (LLMs). First, it identifies and 'flattens' adjacent transformer blocks with high similarity by concatenating their Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) components. Second, it applies structured channel pruning (head removal for MHA and Nyström approximation for MLP) to reduce the widened layers back to their original dimensions. This approach bridges depth and width compression, achieving the inference speedups of layer pruning while retaining the higher performance ceiling of channel pruning.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are supported by a strong combination of theoretical analysis (showing deep layers degenerate into identity mappings) and empirical evaluation across multiple LLM families (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2). The experimental design is sound, benchmarking against state-of-the-art unstructured and structured pruning methods. One minor claim issue: the paper states FlattenGPT 'outperforms all other methods in throughput... and latency' (Section 4.3), but Table 2 shows it exactly ties with SLEB (since the resulting macro-architectures are identical). The advantage over SLEB is purely in task accuracy, which should be clarified.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper excellently contextualizes its contributions within the rapidly growing field of LLM compression. It clearly delineates the trade-offs between depth compression (e.g., ShortGPT, SLEB) and width/channel compression (e.g., SliceGPT, LLM-Pruner), positioning FlattenGPT as a 'best of both worlds' solution. Citations are up-to-date and highly relevant.
strengths: Pedagogical clarity and intuition: The narrative flow is exceptional. The paper builds a compelling story starting from the theoretical 'curse of depth', visually explaining the redundancy (Figure 2), and intuitively introducing the flattening operation (Figure 3) before diving into the math.
Innovative methodology: Fusing adjacent layers before pruning is a highly creative way to preserve learned knowledge that would otherwise be discarded by standard block-dropping methods.

Strong empirical results: FlattenGPT consistently outperforms existing layer-pruning methods (like ShortGPT and SLEB) in zero-shot accuracy and perplexity, maintaining up to 96% of dense performance at 20% sparsity.
weaknesses: Misleading speedup claims relative to depth-pruning baselines: Because FlattenGPT and SLEB result in the exact same macro-architecture, their inference latency and throughput are identical (as shown in Table 2). The text should be revised to emphasize that FlattenGPT matches the SOTA speedups of depth pruning while strictly dominating in accuracy, rather than claiming it 'outperforms' them in speed.

Complexity of the MLP pruning stage: While the Nyström approximation is mathematically justified (Lemma 3.1), it is less intuitively explained for a general audience compared to the MHA head pruning. A brief intuitive explanation of why ridge leverage scores are necessary here would improve accessibility.
questions_for_authors: Could you clarify the phrasing in Section 4.3 regarding throughput and latency outperformance? Would it be more accurate to say FlattenGPT matches the best-in-class acceleration of depth pruning while significantly mitigating the performance degradation?

In Algorithm 1, when flattening layers, how does the method handle the KV-cache during inference for the flattened layers, especially when dealing with Grouped Query Attention (GQA) as mentioned in the Appendix?
How sensitive is the Nyström approximation to the choice of the ridge intensity parameter lambda? Was the specific scaling empirically tuned, or is there a theoretical justification?

summary_of_contributions: The paper proposes FlattenGPT, a fine-grained depth compression method for Large Language Models (LLMs). It addresses the performance degradation typical of entire-layer pruning and the depth/latency-retention issues of channel pruning. The approach works in two stages: (1) Iterative Layer Flattening, which merges highly similar adjacent transformer blocks into a single, wider block, and (2) Channel Pruning, which compresses the merged block back to its original dimensions using Nyström approximation for the MLP and activation-based head pruning for the MHA. This results in a shallower model with consistent architectural dimensions, achieving better accuracy-latency trade-offs than existing depth and width pruning methods.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are well-supported by robust empirical evidence. The authors test on multiple widely-used LLM families (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2) across various sizes (up to 70B parameters). The experimental design is sound, benchmarking against state-of-the-art depth (SLEB, ShortGPT, LaCo) and width (SliceGPT, Wanda) compression methods. The latency and throughput measurements on A100 GPUs convincingly support the claim that FlattenGPT matches the hardware efficiency of depth pruning while maintaining superior performance.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper effectively contextualizes its contribution within both depth compression (layer dropping/merging) and width compression (channel/attention head pruning). It clearly distinguishes FlattenGPT from simple layer merging (e.g., LaCo) by introducing the flattening plus pruning paradigm. The literature review is comprehensive, covering recent and relevant works like SLEB, ShortGPT, and SliceGPT.
strengths: High practical utility and deployability: By compressing the merged layers back to their original architectural dimensions (same number of attention heads and hidden size), the resulting model is a standard, shallower transformer. This guarantees out-of-the-box compatibility with highly optimized inference engines (e.g., vLLM, TensorRT-LLM) without requiring custom CUDA kernels.

Strong empirical performance and efficiency: The method demonstrates a superior Pareto front for accuracy versus latency, outperforming strong baselines like SLEB, ShortGPT, and SliceGPT across multiple modern architectures (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2) up to 70B parameters.

Sound theoretical motivation: The authors provide theoretical analysis (Lemma 2.1 and 2.2) formally explaining the 'curse of depth' and why deeper representations in Pre-LN transformers gravitate toward identity mappings, which perfectly justifies the layer flattening approach.
weaknesses: Lack of generative and complex reasoning evaluations: The empirical validation relies heavily on perplexity and zero-shot multiple-choice tasks (e.g., HellaSwag, PIQA). Evaluating on generative benchmarks (e.g., MT-Bench) and complex reasoning tasks (e.g., GSM8K, HumanEval) would better reflect real-world LLM usage and expose potential degradation in complex generation.

Unexplored domain-specific calibration effects: While the ablation shows robustness to the size of the calibration dataset, the impact of the dataset's domain (e.g., using general text vs. code vs. math) on the preservation of specific model capabilities during the channel pruning phase is not investigated.
questions_for_authors: Can you provide results or insights on how FlattenGPT affects generative performance (e.g., MT-Bench, AlpacaEval) and complex reasoning (e.g., GSM8K) compared to the dense model?

Did you observe any capability-specific degradation (e.g., loss of coding ability) if the calibration dataset (WikiText-2) lacks representation of those domains? Would a diverse calibration mixture improve the Nyström approximation for the MLP pruning?
What is the peak GPU memory requirement during the pruning phase for the LLaMA-2 70B model? Is it feasible to run the pruning pipeline on a standard 8x80GB node without OOM issues?

summary_of_contributions: The paper introduces FlattenGPT, a novel two-stage depth compression method for Large Language Models (LLMs). Instead of entirely dropping redundant transformer blocks, it first merges (flattens) adjacent blocks that exhibit high cosine similarity in their input features. It then applies channel pruning (MHA head pruning and MLP Nyström approximation) to reduce the parameters of the widened, flattened block back to the original architectural dimensions. This approach preserves knowledge better than standard layer pruning and maintains architectural consistency better than standard channel pruning, achieving strong zero-shot and perplexity results on LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, and Baichuan-2.
claims_and_evidence: The claims are generally well-supported by empirical evidence. The paper demonstrates that FlattenGPT outperforms existing training-free depth compression methods (like SLEB, ShortGPT, and LaCo) across multiple LLMs. The ablation studies effectively isolate the benefits of flattening versus pruning. Theoretical claims regarding the curse of depth and Nyström approximation optimality are supported by formal proofs in the appendix. However, the experimental results lack error bars or variance reporting, which makes it slightly difficult to assess the statistical significance of the improvements, particularly for the fine-tuning (RFT) results.
relation_to_prior_work: The paper effectively contextualizes its contributions within the broader literature on LLM compression. It clearly distinguishes FlattenGPT from unstructured pruning, structured width pruning (e.g., SliceGPT, LLM-Pruner), and depth pruning (e.g., ShortGPT, SLEB). The authors effectively argue how their method bridges the gap between depth and width compression. Citations are highly relevant and up-to-date.
strengths: Novel and intuitive perspective on depth compression: by flattening layers instead of dropping them, the model preserves learned knowledge while achieving depth reduction.
Strong empirical results across multiple state-of-the-art LLM families (LLaMA-2/3, Qwen-1.5, Baichuan-2), showing clear improvements over existing depth compression baselines.
Thorough theoretical grounding, providing proofs for why deeper layers exhibit redundancy (curse of depth) and why the chosen Nyström approximation is optimal for the MLP pruning step.
weaknesses: Lack of code provision: For a systems/compression paper, providing the implementation is crucial for reproducibility. No anonymous repository is linked.

Missing complexity analysis: The paper does not provide a formal Big-O analysis of the computational complexity (time and space) for the calibration and pruning algorithms, particularly the correlation matrix inversion.
Lack of variance reporting: The zero-shot and fine-tuning results are presented as point estimates without error bars or standard deviations across multiple random seeds.
questions_for_authors: Will you release the source code and exact scripts used for calibration, pruning, and evaluation to ensure full reproducibility?
What is the theoretical computational complexity (time and space) of calculating the ridge leverage scores and solving the Nyström approximation for the MLP pruning step?
How sensitive is the method to the choice of the ridge intensity hyperparameter lambda (currently set to 10x the mean singular value)? Was a sweep performed to determine this heuristic?
Can you provide variance or error bars for the Recovery Fine-Tuning (RFT) experiments across different random seeds?
